source_text:
Fragmenta in Joannem
1 {3Jο 1, 1}3Ὁ λόγος μίαν οἶδεν ἀρχήν, οὐ δύο, ὡς λέγουσιν οἱ Μανιχαῖοι,
οὐδὲ πρώτου αἴτιον καὶ δεύτερον αἴτιον καὶ τρίτον αἴτιον, ὡς λέγουσι Πλάτων,
Βασιλίδης,Μαρκίων, Ἄρειος, Εὐνόμιος· λέγεται μὲν γὰρ ἀρχὴ ὁ πατὴρ καὶ ἀρχὴ ὁ
υἱὸς καὶ ἀρχὴ τὸ πνεῦμα διὰ τὸ συναΐδιον τῆς τριάδος, οὐ διὰ τὸ τρεῖς εἶναι ἀρχάς,
ἐπεὶ καὶ τὸν πατέρα λέγομεν θεὸν καὶ τὸν υἱὸν θεὸν καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα θεόν, οὐχ ὡς
τρίθεον σέβοντες, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ ὁμοούσιον τῆς μιᾶς θεότητος τῶν τριῶν ὑποστάσεων.
2 {3Jο 1, 1}3Τὴν Σαβελλίου αἵρεσιν διὰ τοῦτο καταβάλλει τὰς ὑποστάσεις σημαίνων
πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ· οὐδὲ γὰρ υἱοπατορίαν ἡ ἐκκλησία δοξάζει καθὰ μυθεύων ὁΛίβυς
εἶπεν.Μίαν ὑπόστασιν λέγουσι τῆς τριάδος Σαβέλλιος, Νοητός, Ναυάτος,
ΠαῦλοςΣαμοσατεύς, Μάρκελλος.Οὐκ ἦν προφορικός, ἀλλ' ἐνυπόστατος καὶ οὐ μόνον
ἐνυπόστατος, ἀλλὰ καὶ θεός.Φωτεινὸς λέγει, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ πατρὸς Λόγος ἀνυπόστατος
ὢν ὡς ὁ ἡμέτερος εἰς σάρκα μετεβλήθη.Ἐπειδὴ ἀκούοντές τινες τῶν αἱρετικῶν, ὅτι ὁ
πατὴρ ἐγέννησε τὸν υἱόν, σκανδαλίζονται ἐννοοῦντες ῥεῦσιν ἢ πάθος γίνεσθαι περὶ
τὸν πατέρα, ἅπερ πέφυκεν ἐπὶ τῶν παχείων σωμάτων ἔσθ' ὅτε συμβαίνειν.
προαναστέλλων αὐτῶν τὴν εὐήθειαν ὁ εὐαγγελιστὴς ἐκ προοιμιῶν τὸν υἱὸν ἅπαξ
καὶ δεύτερον καὶ τρίτον ἐκάλεσε Λόγον, ἵνα τὸ ἀπαθὲς παραστήσῃ τῆς γεννήσεως·
ὡς γὰρ ὁ ἡμέτερος λόγος ἀρρεύστως καὶ ἀμειώτως καὶ ἀπαθῶς γεννᾶται ἐκ τοῦ νοῦ
(ὁμοίως καὶ τὸ ἡμέτερον πνεῦμα), οὕτω καὶ ἡ γέννησις τοῦ υἱοῦ· διὸ καὶ ἐλέχθη·
«Ἐξηρεύξατο ἡ καρδία μου λόγον ἀγαθόν», ὅ ἐστι θεόν, ὃς μόνος «ἐστὶν ἀγαθός». 3
{3Jο 1, 2}3Ἀντὶ τοῦ συναΐδιος ἦν τῷ πατρὶ ἐν τῇ τοῦ πατρὸς ὑπάρχων φύσει, ἔχων
τόπον ἀρχαιότατον τὴν τοῦ γεννήσαντος φύσιν· ἡ γὰρ ἀρχὴ ὑπεραναβαίνει τοὺς
αἰῶνας· ἀρχὴ γὰρ λέγεται ὁ πατὴρ τοῦ υἱοῦ κατὰ μόνον τὸ ἐξ οὗ· τῇ γὰρ αἰτίᾳ ὁ
πατὴρ τοῦ υἱοῦ προεπινοηθήσεται, οὐ μὴν τῇ ὑπάρξει προθεωρηθήσεται. πανταχοῦ
δὲ ἐντίθησι τὸ ἦν παραπέμπων τὸν υἱὸν ἐπὶ τὸ ἄναρχον· οὐ γὰρ εἶπεν ἀρχὴν ἔσχεν,
ἀλλ' ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν. 4 {3Jο 1, 3}3Ἄλλην ἐκβάλλει αἵρεσιν διδάσκων, ὅτι διὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ
ἐκτίσθη πάντα τὰ γενητά, οὐ μὴν δι' ἀγγ
pass_a_gloss: The Logos knows a single principle, not two principles as the Manichaean party asserts, and not a first cause plus a second cause plus a third cause as Plato, Basilides, Marcion, Arius, and Eunomius teach. Father, Son, and Spirit are each called principle because the Trinity is co-eternal, not because three principles exist; we name each person God without worshipping three gods, on account of the one shared Godhead of three hypostases. By marking Father and Son as hypostases he overthrows Sabellius; the church refuses son-fatherhood as the Libyan myth claimed. Sabellius, Noetus, Novatus, Paul of Samosata, and Marcellus teach one hypostasis for the Trinity. The Word was not merely spoken forth; he is hypostatic and God. Photinus holds that an unhypostatic Word from the Father changed into flesh as our speech does. Some heretics stumble at the Father begetting the Son as if generation meant bodily flux or passion; the evangelist forestalls that folly by calling the Son Word repeatedly from the opening, to show passionless generation—like human speech born from mind without drain or passion, and likewise human spirit. Hence the citation: my heart belched a good word, that is God who alone is good. He was co-eternal with the Father in the Father’s nature, and the begetter’s nature is his most ancient place; principle outruns the ages. Father is principle of Son only as the ‘from whom’; cause places Father first in thought, not existence. The repeated ‘was’ drives the Son toward the beginningless: not ‘he began,’ but ‘in the beginning he was.’ Another heresy falls: all generated things were made through the Son, not through good or evil angels as Plato, Simon, Basilides, Nicolas, Menander, the Borborian, Saturnilus, and Cerinthus supposed; hence Saturnilus and the Apostolics ban marriage. The wording stresses that Father and Spirit create with the Son: what the Father does, he works through the Son in the Holy Spirit, and naming one hypostasis implies the rest of the one essence. Whatever the Father made through the Son was made alive from him. The Word did not arise inside a man; by the Spirit he strengthened the virgin, dwelt in her womb as foundation, and built rational ensouled flesh from Mary united to himself—life, as he is life—so partakers are freed from death and corruption into unceasing goods of the coming age, true life. The Only-begotten’s incarnation lights people into true God-knowledge and every virtue by which life-giving—enjoyment of goods—happens. The world is darkness beside inexpressible unapproachable light; yet the Son lights the mind for action, truth always holds, falsehood does not beat truth. pass_b_english: The Word knows one beginning, not two, as the Manichaeans say, nor a first cause and a second cause and a third cause, as Plato, Basilides, Marcion, Arius, and Eunomius say. For the Father is called beginning, and the Son beginning, and the Spirit beginning, because of the co-eternity of the Trinity, not because there are three beginnings; since we also call the Father God and the Son God and the Spirit God, not as worshipping three gods, but because of the consubstantiality of the one Godhead of the three hypostases.

Through this he overthrows Sabellius’s heresy by signifying the hypostases of Father and Son; for the Church does not glorify a son-fatherhood, as the Libyan myth-teller said. Sabellius, Noetus, Novatus, Paul of Samosata, and Marcellus say one hypostasis of the Trinity. He was not uttered-forth, but hypostatic, and not only hypostatic but also God. Photinus says that from the Father a Word without hypostasis, like ours, was changed into flesh. Since some heretics, hearing that the Father begot the Son, take offense and think a flowing or passion happens to the Father—such as naturally sometimes happens with thick bodies—the evangelist, anticipating their folly, from the preface called the Son Word once and twice and thrice, to present the passionlessness of the begetting; for as our word is begotten from the mind without flowing, without diminishment, and without passion (likewise also our spirit), so also is the begetting of the Son. Therefore it was also said: “My heart has belched forth a good word” (Psalm 45:1), which is God, who alone “is good.”

That is: he was co-eternal with the Father, existing in the Father’s nature, having as most ancient place the nature of the one who begot him; for the beginning surpasses the ages. For the Father is called beginning of the Son only according to the “from whom”; for in cause the Father will be conceived before the Son, but not in existence contemplated before him. And everywhere he inserts the “was,” sending the Son on toward the beginningless; for he did not say he had a beginning, but “in the beginning he was” (John 1:1–2).

He casts out another heresy by teaching that through the Son all things that came to be were created, not through good or evil angels, as some wrongly supposed—among them Plato, Simon, Basilides, Nicolas, Menander, the Borborian, Saturnilus, and Cerinthus. Therefore some also forbid marriage and begetting: Saturnilus and the Apostolics.

The wording has emphasis that not the Son alone created all things, but also the Father and the Spirit; for whatever the Father does, he works through the Son in the Holy Spirit, and where one of the three hypostases is said to act, the remaining hypostases of the one essence are conceived with it.
All things whatever the Father made through the Son were made alive from him.

The Word did not come to be in a man, but in a certain way he himself, strengthening the virgin through the Spirit and dwelling in her womb, became a foundation; and in him he built the rational ensouled flesh united to him from Mary, which is life. For as he himself is life, so also is the flesh united to him, of which those who partake are made alive, freed from death and corruption and sent into the enjoyment of the unceasing goods of the age to come, which is truly life.
The incarnation of the Only-begotten leads people by light toward true knowledge of God and toward every kind of virtue, through which life-giving happens, that is, the enjoyment of the goods.

Darkness is the whole world by comparison with the inexpressible and unapproachable light. Yet the Son also enlightens the mind toward what must be done, and truth always prevails; falsehood does not overcome the truth.
